# Paperboat launch checklist

The **only** progress tracker. PLAN.md explains each item (decisions, scope, where to start);
this file records whether it works. Work top to bottom, one section at a time: a feature is
done when **all** its scenario rows and command rows are `[x]` on L and M (Windows after launch, PLAN 1.1; W cells are not in the launch gate). Then the next.

## How to mark

- Section **X. Cross-platform** is different: its three cells are platform pairs (L↔M, L↔W, M↔W), each `[x]` only when verified in both directions between two real devices.

- Cells: **L** = Linux (hp), **M** = macOS (apple), **W** = Windows (victus). For S-sections
  (groundwork, infrastructure, release) only the first cell is used.
- `[ ]` not verified · `[~]` in progress · `[x]` verified on the real device · `[!]` fails
  (write the failure in Evidence) · `n/a` impossible on that platform (say why in Evidence).
- Mark `[x]` **only** with evidence: a smoke-suite test id with its results file
  (`smoke:<id> results/<file>.json`), or the commit plus exact command and result summary
  for a manual check (`manual: <commit> <what was run> → <result>`).
- When a fix changes code, re-verify every `[x]` row of the affected features on all
  platforms; any row that breaks becomes `[!]` and is fixed first (regressions first).
- Commit and push this file together with the work it records.

## Command rows: what `[x]` means

A command row is `[x]` on a platform only when, on that platform: (1) its main use works
against real machines and server with a correct result; (2) every flag in
`cli/docs/cli/<command>.md` behaves as documented (or the doc is fixed); (3) `--json` output,
where supported, is valid; (4) errors are clear for invalid input, missing permission, target
offline and not signed in; (5) `--help` is accurate; (6) it is in the smoke suite when it can
be automated. Hidden/internal commands (e.g. `pb daemon …`) are verified through the flows
that use them; say which in Evidence.

(cli/cmd/pb/ssh_command.go sshWindowsAgentForwardingMessage, kept equal to the check's WINDOWS_AGENT_LIMIT by test_windows_forwarding_asserts_the_limit_message_the_cli_prints_and_never_passes_on_noise) and the session goes on, also for plain `ssh -A`. The agent part is a documented Windows limitation (user decision 2026-11-11): Microsoft's sshd, stock and managed alike, cannot forward an agent into a Windows machine — session.c hardcodes /tmp/ssh-XXX so mkdtemp fails, and the AF_UNIX server bind is then refused (PowerShell/Win32-OpenSSH issues #1461, #1865; maintainers: server-side agent forwarding is not supported). macOS [x] 2026-11-04: ssh_mac_rows.py --only forwarding, macl -> apple (dev-d6f2689c) PASS: -L port forward, -A agent forward, no X11 for plain ssh and pb ssh. ## X. Cross-platform

Behaviour that only matters when platforms mix. The three cells are platform **pairs**, not platforms: **L↔M** (Linux and macOS), **L↔W** (Linux and Windows), **M↔W** (macOS and Windows). A pair is `[x]` only when the check passed in **both directions** between two real devices of those platforms (A→B and B→A), with the exact evidence named in the Evidence column; single-platform behaviour stays in F1–F15. Pair devices: L = hp / pbvm* / ubuntu24, M = apple, W = victus. Rows are written from how the code actually works (config sync: `cli/internal/hostruntime/configsync`; layers, path rules and manifest limits are quoted where they decide the check). Windows pairs follow the launch gate rules (PLAN 1.1): they are checked after launch.

**How config sync layers work today (so the rows below match it).** Four sources are merged in this order, later wins per field: the shared file `.paperboat/config-sync.toml` in the repository, its `[os.linux]`, `[os.darwin]` or `[os.windows]` section for the machine's OS, its `[machine.<name>]` section (`<name>` is the machine's Paperboat name from `pb machine list`), then the machine's own file (`pb config sync path`; it may not contain `[os.*]` or `[machine.*]`). Fields: `enabled`, `mode`, `automatic_updates`, `[pull]`/`[push]` (`repository_id`, `url`, `branch`), `[paths."<repository path>"]` (`local_path`, `kind = file|directory`, `include`, `exclude`). `~`, `$XDG_CONFIG_HOME`, `%APPDATA%`, `%LOCALAPPDATA%` and `%USERPROFILE%` expand only when written and available; a missing variable fails. Content is never converted (no line-ending, charset or template step). Only regular files sync (`unsupported_file_type` otherwise); the only mode kept is "executable or not". A `[machine.<name>]` that matches none of the account's machines is a warning in `validate`/`apply` (text and `--json` `warnings`); a machine whose name the daemon does not know yet keeps sync paused instead of guessing (the server sends the name as `machine_alias`, 952fe7b3). There is no per-architecture or per-distribution OS key. Rows X-02 and X-12 record what exists.

| ID | Scenario (what is checked, and how) | L↔M | L↔W | M↔W | Evidence |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| X-01 | Config sync, same repository file, different destinations per OS: a shared `.paperboat/config-sync.toml` maps `settings.json` with `[os.linux.paths]`, `[os.darwin.paths]` and `[os.windows.paths]` (`~/.config/…`, `~/Library/Application Support/…`, `%APPDATA%/…`) for both `kind = "file"` and `kind = "directory"` (with `include`/`exclude`). | X-38 | Direct and relay paths between OSes (F9-05, F21-49, F21-51): two machines of different OSes behind different NATs reach each other directly where possible and through a relay otherwise (`pb ping` states the path; UDP blocked forces relay), with the host firewall on each OS in its default state (Windows Defender Firewall prompts and rules, macOS application firewall and PF, ufw, firewalld or nftables on L) and no prompt left waiting; dual-stack, IPv6-only, a full-tunnel VPN (Tailscale, WireGuard, corporate) on one side, a captive portal, a Wi-Fi switch and a NAT rebinding recover on their own; the system proxy (macOS network settings, Windows WinHTTP/WinINET, `http_proxy` for a Linux service) is honoured or its absence named by the daemon, which runs with a different environment than the user's shell on every OS. | [ ] | [ ] | [ ] | — |
| X-39 | Reachability by service model (F1-07, F1-11, F2-05): each OS keeps the machine reachable from the other OSes in the states its service model allows and names the states it does not: Linux with no login and after logout (linger), macOS before the first login after boot and with FileVault, with fast user switching and a locked screen, Windows as a service before sign-in, after logout, with fast startup, hibernation and an RDP session; after each event `pb wait --for runtime`, `--for transport` and `--for ssh` from the other OS report the truth, `pb service status` agrees, a reboot brings the machine back without user action, and `pb exec` from the other OS works at the documented point. | [ ] | [ ] | [ ] | — |
| X-40 | Machine names across OSes (F2-04, F5-04, F9-01): a machine name is valid as a DNS label and as a file name on every OS: names with spaces, underscores, Unicode, uppercase (macOS "Alice's MacBook" and Windows computer names), 63 characters or more, `CON` and other reserved names are normalised or refused with a clear message at enroll and rename; two names that differ only by case are one name; `pb machine rename` on one OS updates the ssh aliases, local names, `known_hosts` entries, tunnel and config-sync references and shell completion on the other OSes (config sync pauses as in X-02, local access names move); a stale alias is never accepted for a different machine. | [ ] | [ ] | [ ] | — |
| X-41 | Removal seen from another OS (F1-09, F1-10, F2-05): when a machine of one OS is uninstalled, reset or revoked, the machines of the other OSes show it gone or offline with the reason at once; their ssh aliases, local names, ENV delivery, tunnels, previews, config-sync entries, shared sessions and open flows to it end or are cleaned (nothing keeps retrying in a tight loop); pairing the same machine again after `pb reset` gives a new identity that the other OS trusts only after `pb ssh trust-host` or a fresh enrollment, never a silent host-key change; removing a machine of one OS leaves nothing behind in the account that the other OS still depends on. | [ ] | [ ] | [ ] | — |
| X-42 | Reachability checks and diagnostics across OSes (F4-05, F15-01, F15-02, F15-05): `pb ping` and `pb wait --for runtime|transport|ssh` from each OS to each other OS report the same path and conditions in text and `--json`; `pb doctor` on each side names a peer problem (clock, relay, firewall, proxy) in the same words; a `pb bugreport` made on W opens on L and M (archive names, long paths, Unicode, CRLF logs) and one made on L or M opens on W, holds no secrets, ENV values, terminal or file contents (also not in Windows or macOS user paths), and its support reference resolves; shell completion for bash, zsh, fish and PowerShell completes machine names that contain non-ASCII characters or hyphens on each OS. | [ ] | [ ] | [ ] | — |

## F21. Robustness (PLAN 3b gaps)

Everything on the Reliability, scale and efficiency card except the Performance section (P). Grouped by what breaks:
network and outage recovery, core access contracts, the client daemon (install, update, service), Windows security,
edge and tunnel, server data, server runtime and limits, health and code health, scale. Row ids are stable (code and
PLAN refer to them), so rows are grouped, not renumbered. A row is `[x]` only when its named test passes on the
pushed build; device cells need the named smoke check on that platform. Audit rows (F21-63..156) come from the four
code audits (A core access, B edge and tunnel, C install and update, D server data), the duplicated-contracts audit
and the open review lows; Windows-only and macOS-only findings have `n/a` on the other platforms.
